Vs.
Md. Mizanur Rahman & anr ------ Opposite Party.
full_judgment:
Md Joynul Abedin J: This Rule at the instance of the plaintiff-petitioner was issued under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure calling upon the defendant opposite party No. 1 to show cause as to why the judgment and decree dated 2-7-02 passed by the Additional District Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 233 of 2000 reversing the judgment and decree dated 15-5-2000 passed by the 6th Assistant Judge in Title Suit No. 214 of 1997 decreeing the suit should not be set aside.

2. The plaintiff-petitioner and two other plaintiff’s by filing the aforesaid suit sought for a declaration that the ex parte judgment and decree dated 5-6-97 passed in Title Suit No. 103 of 1996 by the Assistant Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka is untenable, void and not binding upon them contending, inter alia that the suit land originally belonged to one Krishna Chandra Dutta and thereafter one Shaila Bala Devi. Defendant No. 2 Mohibur Rahman became the owner of the suit property on the basis of a registered deed of permanent lease dated 27-2-52 from said Shaila Bala Devi. Since said Mohibur Rahman was a non-Bengali, he left Bangladesh in 1971. Accordingly, the suit property was declared and taken over as abandoned property and the plaintiff-petitioner and two other plaintiffs were given lease by the Government as an abandoned property on 2-3-78 and at the time of granting lease the Government also realised the compensatory rents from the plaintiffs including the plaintiff-petitioner since 1-1-72. The suit property was subsequently enlisted in the KA list in the Bangladesh Gazette, Extra Ordinary dated 23-9-1986. The defendant-opposite party No. 1 by filing Title Suit No. 103 of 1996 fraudulently obtained an ex parte decree dated 5-6-97 in the said suit without disclosing the abandoned character of the suit land and without impleading the plaintiff-petitioner and two other plaintiffs.

3. The opposite party No. 1 as defendant No. 1 in the suit contested the same by filing written statement contending, inter alia, that the suit was not maintainable and was also barred by limitation. It was further contended that defendant No. 2, Mahibur Rahman, was the owner of the suit land and he as the owner in possession mortgaged the same in his favour by taking Taka 30(thirty) thousand from him and executed the mortgage deed and also inducted him into the possession of the suit property. During the period of liberation war the defendant-opposite party No. 1 was dispossessed by some miscreants. After the liberation of Bangladesh defendant-opposite party No. 1 came back to the suit property and found out that some of the persons of the original owner of the mortgaged property were in possession. He then asked Mahibur Rahman either to give him back the mortgage money with interest or to restore possession of the suit property to him. Said Mahibur Rahman then requested the defendant opposite party No. 1 to allow him time up to the due date for return of the mortgage money and if he then failed to pay back the mortgage money, he would register the necessary document in his favour and restore possession to him. In spite of the aforesaid promise the said mortgagor Mahibur Rahman failed to pay him the mortgage money as per his promise. The defendant-opposite party No. 1 then filed the said suit for foreclosure being Title Suit No. 103 of 1996 impleading the said mortgagor, Mohibur Rahman, and also the Government, represented by the Deputy Commissioner, Dhaka.

4. Summons in the suit were served upon the defendants and the Government entered appearance and filed written statement. The Government as defendant No. 2 filed an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure for rejection of the plaint, inter alia, on the ground that the suit property was an abandoned property and, as such, the suit was not maintainable. The trial Court however, by order dated 1-6-97 rejected the aforesaid application on the ground that the Government being a pro forma defendant, as no relief was sought against it was not competent to file such an application under Order VII, rule 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The Government neither challenged the said order before any higher forum nor contested the suit. The said suit for foreclosure was however, decreed ex parte in favour of the defendant-opposite party No. 1. Defendant opposite party No. 1 then put the decree into execution and when warrant for possession was issued by the executing Court the plaintiff-petitioner as well as the Government got the execution proceeding stayed.

5. In this background of the case, the trial Court having recorded the evidence of both the sides and on consideration of the materials on record decreed the suit. The defendant-opposite party No. 1 being aggrieved preferred Title Appeal No. 433 of 2000 before the Additional District Judge, 6th Court, Dhaka. The appellate Court below thereafter on due scrutiny of facts and law overturned the impugned judgment and decree passed by the trial Court by dismissing the suit mainly, on the ground that since the plaintiff-petitioner did not seek any declaration as to his lease-hold right, his suit for mere declaration that the ex parte decree passed in the suit for foreclosure (Title Suit No. 103 of 1996) was hit by section 42 of the Specific Relief Act.

6. Mr Mansur Habib, the learned Advocate appearing for the plaintiff-petitioner, vehemently contends that since the plaintiff-petitioner was a lessee under the Government of the suit property as abandoned property, suit for a mere declaration that ex parte decree dated 5-6-97 obtained by defendant-opposite-party No. 1, in the aforesaid foreclosure suit was very much maintainable under section 42 of the Specific Relief Act even if he omitted to seek for any declaration as to his leasehold right as to the suit property. In support of this contention, Mr Mansur Habib referred to the decision in the case of Moulvi Abdul Mannan vs Md Rafiqul Islam, reported in 46 DLR 493 and also the case of Jinnat Ali vs Muktear Abdul Mojid reported in 27 DLR 385.

7. On the other hand, Mr S Rashed Jahangir, the learned Advocate, appearing for the defendant-opposite party No. 1, submits that since the plaintiff-petitioner merely sought for a declaration that the ex parte decree dated 5-6-97 passed in Title Suit No. 103 of 1996 was fraudulent and not binding on him without seeking any declaration that he has lease-hold right in the suit property, the suit was not maintainable under secti6r) 42 of the Specific Relief Act, inasmuch as such declaration may be regarded not as a main relief but as a consequential relief. In other wards it is submitted that without praying for any main relief as designated under section 42 a mere consequential relief as in the present case will not render the suit maintainable. The case of Ishaque Miah vs Abdul Mozid Mollah and others reported in 48 DLR 465 and the case of Munsur Ali Mullick vs Nurul Haque Mullick reported in 1986 BCR (AD) 56 are cited in support of this contention.

8. It may be advisable to reproduce section 42 of the Specific Relief Act for proper appreciation of the contentions advanced by both the parties.

"42 Discretion of Court as to Declaration of Status or Right: Any person entitled to any legal character, or to any right as to any property, may institute a suit against any person denying, or interested to deny, his title to such character or right, and the court may in its discretion make therein a declaration that he is so entitled, and the plaintiff need not in such suit ask for any further relief.

Bar to such Declaration: Provided that no Court shall make any such declaration where the plaintiff, being able to seek further relief than a mere declaration of title, omits to do so."

Careful examination of the language used in the aforesaid section shows that the plaintiff must seek for a declaration as to his right to the suit property as a substantive or main relief. If such substantive relief fails to provide for a complete relief without praying for something more as a consequential relief, such consequential relief must be sought for. In the absence of such consequential relief, suit for declaration of his right to property in question would not be maintainable. But where, in view of the dispute involved, further prayer by way of consequential relief is not considered necessary, suit with a simple prayer for substantive relief, such as a prayer for declaration of plaintiff's title to the suit land is enough to maintain a suit where prayer for recovery of possession is not necessary as he is already in possession.

<u>9. In the instant case, the plaintiff-petitioner admittedly did not seek for any declaration by way of substantive relief that he was a lessee to the suit property under the Government as an abandoned property or otherwise. In the absence of any prayer for such substantive relief the trial Court below was not competent in law merely to give a decree as regards the consequential relief that the decree dated 5-6-97 passed in Title Suit No. 103 of 1996 was fraudulent, void and not binding on the plaintiff-petitioner.</u>

10. To sum up, it is stated that in the present case the plaintiff-petitioner was required first to pray for a declaration as a substantive relief that he was a lessee to the suit property under the Government as an abandoned property and then for a further declaration, as a consequential relief, that the ex parte decree dated 5-6-97 passed in Title Suit No. 103 of 1996 in relation to the said lease-hold was fraudulent, void and not binding on him. This view finds support in the aforesaid two cases (48 DLR 465 and 1986 BCR (AD) 56) cited by the defendant-opposite party No. 1. There is, therefore, no justification to interfere with the impugned judgment and decree passed by the lower appellate Court on sound exposition of law and the same is accordingly affirmed.

In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to costs.

End.

parties:

Vs.

full_judgment:
Gour Gopal Saha, J: This Rule is directed against the judgment and decree dated 22.6.1989 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 4 of 1988 affirming the judgment and decree dated 31.3.1987 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 391 of 1983 dismissing the suit.

2. The plaintiff's Case, in short, is that he joined the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation, Krishi Bhaban, on 18.12.1965 as a Lower Division Clerk. Subsequently he was posted as Clark-Cum-Store-Keeper on 1.9.1966 in Grade No. III. Thereafter he was promoted as a Senior Store-Keeper in Grade No. II on 2.1.1978 and posted at the office of the Manager, Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation, Dhaka and got the charge of the Movement Transit Godown No. 1 at Narayanganj. The Movement Officer posted at Narayanganj brought baseless charges of negligence of duty, in-subordination and corrupt practices against the plaintiff and asked him to show cause by a notice vide Memo No. 1457 Dated 21.6.1978 and placed him under suspension, He replied to the said show cause notice denying all the allegations brought against him. Thereafter Mr. Mofizul Islam, the District Manager, B.A.D.C. was appointed Enquiry Officer to enquire into the charges brought against him.

3. The plaintiff filed written objection to the appropriate authority against the appointment of the Enquiry Officer but it was rejected. The plaintiff thereafter filed an appeal against the said order before the Member-Director but it was of no avail. Thereafter the plaintiff was dismissed from service by the impugned order dated 5.10.78 on the basis of the illegal and motivated Enquiry Report, without giving him adequate opportunity to defend himself. It was further alleged that no second show-cause notice was served on him before passing the impugned order of dismissal.

4. Thereafter plaintiff-petitioner preferred an appeal before the Chairman, Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation but was unsuccessful and this necessitated the filing of Title Suit No. 64 of 1979 in the Court of Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka challenging the impugned order of dismissal and he obtained a decree therein. Defendant Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation filed an appeal against the aforesaid judgment and decree in the Court of the learned District Judge, Dhaka being Title Appeal No. 56 of 1981. The said appeal was eventually heard by the learned Additional District Judge, Second Court, Dhaka who was pleased to allow the appeal and dismiss the suit. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree the plaintiff thereafter preferred Civil Revision No. 1878 of 1981 before the High Court Division and the said Rule was eventually made absolute and the judgment and decree passed by the learned Court of appeal below were set-aside and decree passed by the trial Court was restored. The defendant then filed Civil Appeal No. 139 of 1982 before the Appellate Division which was ultimately allowed and the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1878 of 1981 were set aside and the judgment and decree passed by the First Appellate Court were affirmed and the suit dismissed.

5. Thereafter the plaintiff served notice upon the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation as required under Section 74 of the Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation Ordinance, 1961 and filed the present suit alleging inter-alia that the enquiry was illegal and he was not given any opportunity to defend himself. It was further alleged that the Enquiry Officer, in connivance with the Chairman of the B.A.D.C., submitted an illegal and motivated report against him on the basis of which the impugned order of dismissal was passed.

6. The defendant Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation by filing written statement denied all the material allegations of the plaint and contended inter alia that charges of indiscipline, in-subordination, negligence of duties and corrupt practices brought against the plaintiff were properly enquired into by a duly appointed Enquiry Officer after meeting all the legal formalities. The plaintiff was given sufficient opportunity to defend himself. The Enquiry Report showed that all the charges brought against him were fully substantiated. The authority on consideration of the Enquiry Report and other materials on record found him guilty of misconduct and rightly passed the order of dismissal. It was further contended that the plaintiff earlier filed Title Suit No. 64 of 1979 before the 1st Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka challenging his order of dismissal dated 5.10.1978 and obtained decree therein on merit. On appeal by the defendant the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court were set-aside and suit was dismissed against which the plaintiff petitioner preferred Civil Revision No.1878 of 1981 before the High Court Division Eventually the said rule was made absolute, the impugned judgment and decree passed by the learned Court of appeal below were set-aside and the suit was decreed. Thereafter the defendant filed Civil Appeal No. 139 of 198; before the Appellate Division. The said appeal was allowed and the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1878 of 1981 were set-aside and judgment and decree passed by the first appellate Court were restored and the suit dismissed. It was further contended that since the matter was finally decided on merit by the Appellate Division the present suit on the same cause of action is clearly barred under Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure. It was also contended that the suit is barred by limitation as it was filed long after 3(three) years of the accrual of the cause of action which arose on 5.10.78.

7. The learned Subordinate Judge on consideration of the evidence on record was pleased to dismiss the suit holding that the suit is barred by limitation and it is hit by the principle of res-judicata.

8. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge the plaintiff-petitioner filed an appeal before the learned District Judge, Dhaka being Title Appeal No. 4 of 1988. The appeal was heard by the learned Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka who was pleased by his impugned judgment and decree dated 22.6.89 to dismiss the appeal and to affirm the judgment and decree passed by the learned trial Court Against the aforesaid judgment and decree the plaintiff-petitioner moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

9. Syed Badrul Alam, the learned Counsel appearing for the petitioner, submitted that the learned Court of appeal below erred in law in passing the impugned judgment as the suit was not hit by the principle of res-judicata in view of the fact that the earlier suit, being Title Suit No. 64 of 1979, was dismissed not on merit but on technical grounds. He further submitted that the learned Court of appeal below was also wrong in dismissing the suit on the ground of limitation.

10. Mr. Md. Shamsur Rahman, the learned Counsel appearing for the opposite party, submitted that the plaintiff's earlier Title Suit No. 64 of 1979 was ultimately dismissed .on merit and not on technical grounds and as such the learned Court of appeal below was perfectly justified in dismissing the suit as being hit by the principle of res-judicata. The learned Counsel further submitted that the plaintiff's suit is also clearly. barred by limitation being filed after 3 years of accrual of the cause of action and as such the learned Court of appeal below did not commit any illegality in passing the impugned judgment.

11. We have gone through the impugned judgment passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 4th Court, Dhaka, in Title Appeal No. 4 of 1988 and the judgment passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 391 of 1983. The learned Additional District Judge on consideration of the evidence on record, particularly the evidence of the petitioner as P.W.1 and the evidence of D.W.1 Mr. Mojibur Rahman, Project Director of Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation, found that the plaintiff's earlier suit, being Title Suit No. 56 of 1981, was decreed on contest by the trial Court and the said decree was set aside on merit by the appellate Court in Title Appeal No. 56 of 1981 and the suit was dismissed. Against the aforesaid judgment and decree the petitioner preferred Civil Revision No.1878 of 1981 before the High Court Division which set aside the judgment and decree passed by the Court of appeal below and restored the judgment and decree passed by the trial Court.

12. The defendant opposite party Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation filed an appeal, being Civil Appeal No. 139 of 1982, before the Appellate Division and the learned Appellate Division was pleased the set aside the judgment and order passed by the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 1878 of 1981 and restored the judgment and decree passed by the learned Additional District Judge, Second Court, Dhaka in Title Appeal No. 56 of 1981. The learned Court of appeal below also found that the present suit and the earlier suit filed by the plaintiff were on the same cause of action. Since the matter was finally decided on merit by the learned Appellate Division the present suit is clearly hit by the principle of res-judicata. The learned Additional District Judge also found that the plaintiff was dismissed from service by order dated 5.10.78 and the present suit was filed on 26.12.83 and as such it is clearly barred by limitation. The learned Additional District Judge in support of his conclusion referred to the case of Bangladesh Agricultural Development Corporation Vs. Md. Mannaf Hussain Khan and ors. reported in 36 D.L.R. (A.D.) 69 in which it has been held that when a suit against the Corporation is not filed within 2(two) months from the date of notice served upon the Corporation or any of its officers it will be barred by time. It was also held that such a suit must be filed within 6(six) months of the accrual of the cause of action.

13. In the present case, it is evident that the cause of action of the present suit arose on 5.10.78 when the plaintiff was dismissed from service. The present suit was filed on 26.12.83 i.e. more than 3 years after the accrual of the cause of action and on such consideration the learned Court of appeal below as well as the learned trial Court were perfectly justified in dismissing the suit on the ground of limitation.

14. Section 11 of the Code of Civil Procedure reads as follows:-

"No Court shall try any suit or issue in which the matter directly and substantially in issue has been directly and substantially in issue in a former suit between the same parties, or between parties under whom they or any of them claim litigating under the same title, in a court competent to try such subsequent suit or the suit in which such issue has been subsequently raised, and has been heard and finally decided by such Court".

<u>15. The main object of the principle of res-judicata is to prevent multiplicity of suits and interminable disputes between the litigants. The principle of res-judicata is intended not only to prevent a new decision but also to prevent a new investigation so that the same person cannot be vexed again and again in multiple proceedings over the same question. This principle is mutual in character and it is open as much to the plaintiff as to the defendant.</u>

16. The petitioner has placed no material before us and to prove that the plaintiff's earlier suit being Title Suit No. 64 of 1979 of the Court of the Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Dhaka was not dismissed on merit but it was, in fact, dismissed on a mere technical ground and the issues involved in the present suit were not tried and decided in the previous suit. Since the learned Courts below as courts of facts and on consideration of the evidence on record concurrently found that the present suit is barred by res-judicata as well as by limitation, we find no illegality in the impugned judgment.

17. In the face of the concurrent findings of facts and the proposition of law enunciated by their Lordships in the case reported in 36 DLR(AD) 69 we are satisfied that the Court of appeal below was perfectly justified in dismissing the suit on the ground of limitation as well as on the ground of res-judicata. We do not find any illegality in the impugned judgment calling for interference by us exercising jurisdiction under section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

18. In the result, the Rule is discharged without any order as to cost. The judgment and decree passed by the learned Courts below are affirmed.

Send down the lower Court records at once.

End.

Sharif Uddin Chaklader J: This Rule, at the instance of defendant, directed against judgment and decree dated 7-11-2012 passed by the learned Additional District Judge, 3rd Court, Khulna Allowing Title Appeal No. 401 of 1997 thereby decreeing Title Suit No. 200 of 1980 on reversing those dated 5-10-1997 passed by the learned the then Sub-ordinate Judge now Joint District Judge, 1st Court, Khulna.

2. Mr Fida M Kamal, learned Advocate at the outset submits that, the suit is not maintainable on two grounds at first, the present suit is barred by limitation which was filed long after the period of limitation which can be seen from cause of action of the suit and secondly, Court while allowing the prayer for withdrawal of the suit on 7-4-1980 directed to pay Taka 500 to contesting defendant as condition precedent which having not been paid on the date of institution of the instant suit, this suit cannot proceed.

3. Plaintiff opposite party No. 1 instituted Title Suit No. 200 of 1980 in the court of Sub-ordinate Judge, 1st Court, Khulna against petitioners and others for establishment of title and recovery of khas possession and compensation on the allegation contending inter alia that the land under CS khatian No. 1001 of Mouza Baniakhamar, Police Station Khulna, District Khulna originally belonged to Poilan Sheikh, Badulla Sheikh and Shahamatullah Sheikh in equal share in rayioti right and their names were recorded properly. Of them, Shahamatullah was in exclusive possession of plot No. 3642, Badullah in plot No. 3643 and Ahadullah Sheikh and others were in possession in plot No. 3644 as a right of exchange and their names were mentioned in remark column in the khatian that there was an exchange in between Ahadullah Sheikh and Poilan Sheikh and Ahadullah Sheikh got the land of plot No. 3644; Rahamatullah and others filed Title Suit No. 184 of 1914 and in that suit Ahadullah Sheikh and others were defendant Nos. 1-3 and Poilan Sheikh and others were defendant Nos. 4-10 and they compromised by filing compromise petition separately and in that suit the exchange of Ahadullah Sheikh was admitted and the land Poilan Sheikh got, was admitted; the land which Poilan Sheikh got was again exchanged with Kutubullah Sheikh and others and transferred the land of plot No. 3644 to Heralal Datta by kabala dated 13-9-1927; on the same date, Heralal Datta transferred 1.20 acres of land by patta to Ismail Sheikh including the suit land; for arrears of rent, Heralal Datta filed Rent Suit No. 1782 of 1942 in the court of the then Munsif, 3rd Court, Khulna, the said suit was dismissed for non prosecution. It is further case of plaintiffs that Ismail Sheikh had title over the suit land of plot Nos. 3671 and 3670/4246 under CS khatian No. 2666 and the said land has been situated adjacent south-east side of the suit land; in the year 1954 AD Ismail Sheikh reconstructed the houses on the suit plot and also constructed more 3 rooms and those were tenanted and thereafter, he shifted his house on the land of plot Nos. 3671 and 2670/4246. In SA record the suit land was recorded in SA khatian No. 1015 and the tenant, defaulted to pay rent and Ismail Sheikh filed two SCC Suit being Nos. 108 of 1958 and 71 of 1059 and those were decreed. Momin Mollik also defaulted to pay rent and the landlord, Ismail Sheikh filed Money Suit No. 12 of 1960 and the suit was decreed. Momin Mollik filed Money Suit No. 34 of 1960 which was allowed and thereafter, defendant Nos. 1-6 got possession of the suit land and houses there on. Thereafter, Ismail Sheikh filed Title Suit No. 263 of 1966 which was transferred to the court of Sub-ordinate Judge, Additional Court, Khulna and the same was dismissed. Against which Ismail Sheikh filed Appeal from Original Decree No. 127 of 1976 before in the High Court Division of the Supreme Court of Bangladesh. The suit having running with formal defects, plaintiffs of that suit filed application for withdrawal of the suit with permission to sue afresh. The application was allowed on 7-4-1980. Before that date, the instant suit was filed on 13-3-1980. Momena Bibi and Jomiron Nessa transferred some decimals of land from plot No. 3643 along with other land to Heralal Datta by Kabala dated 9-6-1931 and thereafter, the said land was transferred to Paban Sheikh, son of Poilan Sheikh by a registered lease deed on 26-3-1942 and on that deed there was a statement that Ismail Sheikh is in possession on plot No. 3644 and adjacent west side of plot No. 3643. Title suit No. 208 of 1961 filed by heirs of Shahamatullah was dismissed and in that suit, right of Ismail Sheikh was admitted that the suit land was investigated. Title suit No. 33 of 1963 was filed by defendant Nos. 1-6, was dismissed for default, hence the suit.

4. In the suit the predecessor of these petitioners as defendant Nos. 1 and 6 contested by filing written statement contending inter alia that, remark column of the CS khatian showing amaze possession of Ahadullah in respect of plot No. 3644 is wrong as there was no amaze with Ahadullah Sheikh.

5. Trial court dismissed the suit holding that plaintiffs failed to prove the factum of dispossession on 12-2-1962 and possession before that date; it has been proved that no exchange could be possible; the report of Commissioner in another suit cannot be treated as evidence of another suit without examining the Commissioner. Title Suit No. 263 of 1966 was filed on 16-5-1966 for khas possession and it was alleged that the plaintiffs were dispossessed on 12-6-1962 and thereafter the said suit was renumbered as Title Suit No. 65 of 1971 and when the matter was pending before the High Court Division and application for withdrawal of the suit to file afresh was filed on 11-3-1980 but though the instant suit was filed on 10-3-1980 but it will be treated that the suit was filed on 7-4-1980 and since the date of dispossession on 12-6-1962 the instant suit is barred by limitation. Appellate Court allowed the appeal and decreed the suit on the finding that the Commissioner's report was acceptable, that the suit is not barred by limitation.

6. Mr Fida M Kamal, learned Advocate, submits that, trial court on consideration of the fact of the given case found that in First Appeal No. 127 of 1976 application for withdrawal of the suit with liberty to sue afresh was allowed on 7-4-1980 if it is not otherwise barred by limitation and the cause of action being runs from 1966, the present suit having filed in 1980 is barred by law of limitation. Second point urged by the learned Advocate is that as the High Court Division directed for payment at Taka 500 as condition precedent that having not been done present suit cannot proceed. Learned Advocate further submits that present suit was filed on 13-3-1980 before withdrawal of the suit on 7-4-1980, the cause of action runs having been same two suits cannot run between the same parties side by side for the same relief.

7. Mr Moudud Ahmed, learned Advocate with Mr. Ahmed Nowshed Jamil, appearing for the plaintiff-appellant-opposite parties, on the other hand, submits that, at the time of preparation of the plaint some material facts were not mentioned in the plaint in inadvertence, for the ends of justice the plaint is required to be amended by way of inserting the left out facts but the aforesaid application for amendment of the pleading placed before this Court was not mooted. Learned Advocate further submits that since the present suit having been filed as per order of this Court within time, the suit cannot be dismissed as bar by limitation as such the learned Judge of the appellate Court committed no illegality in allowing the appeal.

8. Let us proceed with our judgment.

9. While Title Suit No. 337 of 1963 was withdrawn on 7-4-1980 in allowing application for withdrawal filed in Appeal From Original Decree No. 127 of 1976 the High Court Division passed the order as:—

"Heard the learned Advocate and perused the application. For the reasons stated in the application it appears that the appellant has made out a case that the suit suffers from formal defects and, as such, the praher for withdrawal of the suit and appeal with liberty to sue afresh, if not the claim is otherwise barred, appears to be or substance. We accept the petition and the plaintiffs are allowed to withdraw the suit and the appeal on condition of depositing a consolidated cost of Taka 500 (Taka Five hundred) only to the contesting defendants before the trial Court and we made it a condition precedent for institution of the contemplated fresh suit. Accordingly, the judgment and decree of the learned Subordinate Judge are set aside and the suit is allowed to be withdrawn on the ground of formal defects with permission to sue afresh, if not otherwise barred subject to payment of cost of Taka 500 (Taka five hundred) only to the contesting defendants before the trial Court."

10. A reading of the order book of the Court of the instant suit we do not find any payment made by the plaintiffs, as such, it may be safely said condition precedent has not been fulfilled.

11. What is condition precedent?

12. Condition implies some state of affairs or events on the happenings of which an obligation attaches called condition precedent. Wharton's Law Lexicon, 1976 Reprint Edition at page 224 it is defined as an event upon which a right under contract or to property may arise, become altered or cease. In their primary meaning, condition precedent are events but for the happenings of which rights will not arise. Condition Precedents Adimpleri Debet Priesquam sequator Effectus a condition precedent must be fulfilled before the effect can follow."

<u>13. Halsbury's Laws of England, 3rd Edition, Volume 8 page 194-of the view 'a condition may be either precedent or subsequent. A condition precedent is fulfilled if it is substantially complied with.'</u>

<u>14. As such when an order was passed an order as condition precedent that must be complied before stepping further. In the instant suit, it is an admitted position that court's verdict has not been complied with before institution of the suit as such the present suit is not maintainable.</u>

15. On the 2nd question i.e. on limitation. We have gone through the reliefs claimed in suit. In the present suit plaintiffs sought for.

“(ক) বিরোধীয় ভূমিতে এওয়াজ সূত্রে বাদী গনের স্বাদশ বর্ষের উর্ধকাল দখল জনিত স্বত্ব সাব্যস্ত পূর্বক বিবাদীগনকে গৃহাদি হইতে উচ্ছেদ ক্রমে খাস দখলের ডিক্রী দিতে মর্জি হয় ।

(খ) যে দখলের তারিখ হইতে বাদী গন যে ওয়াশিলাত পাইতে অধিকারী তাহা সাব্যস্ত হয় এবং তদবাবদ কোর্ট ফি গ্রহণে ওয়াশিলাতের ডিক্রী দিতে মর্জি হয়৷”

16. In the earlier suit, plaintiffs sought relief for declaration of title and for recovery of khas possession. Two suits are for two different district relief but cause of action has been shown as same. In earlier suit title by adverse possession was claimed but in the instant suit, recovery of khas possession has been sought for. Question is when plaintiffs were dispossessed. But curious enough that no fresh cause of action has been shown. Let us see the application for amendment of the plaint put forwarded before us by learned Advocate for the opposite parties, we may quote the relevant portion of the application of the amendment of the plaint which runs as follows:—

প্রকাশ থাকে যে, এফ, এ নং ১২৭/৭৬ চলাকালীন ঐ মাকদ্দমার ৯-২০ নং বিবাদীগন অর্থাৎ বাণীর অধিনন্থ বিশ্বাস ঘাতক ভাড়াটিয়া গন বুঝিতে পারে যে উচ্ছেদ মোকদ্দমায় দায় তাহাদেরকে বহন করিতে হইবে এবং খেসারত দিতে হইবে। ঐ দায় এড়াইবার উদ্দেশ্যে তাহারা রাতের অন্ধকারে গত ইং ১-৩-১৯৭৯ তারিখে নালিশী জমি ত্যাগ করিয়া চলিয়া যায়। ঐ রাতেই শুন্য ঘরে অত্র মোকদ্দমার ১০ ও ১১ নং বিবাদী প্রবেশ করিয়া পরিবার পরিজনসহ বসবাস শুরু করে । এই ঘটনা দেখিয়া বাদী তাহাদেরকে ঘর ছাড়িয়া দিতে বলিলে তাহারা বাদীকে নিয়মিত ভাড়া দিয়া ঘরে বসবাস করার অনুমতি চায়৷ অন্য কোন উপায় না পাইয়া বাদী তাহাতে সম্মত হন ৷ মাস পার হইলে নতুন ভাড়াটিয়া ১০-১১ নংৰিবাদীর নিকট বাদী ৪-৪-১৯৭৯ তারিখে ভাড়া তলব করিলে তাহারা ১-৬ নং বিবাদীর গোপন ইন্ধনে বাদীকে ভাড়া দিতে অস্বীকার করেন ৷ ফলে ঐ সময় চলমান এফ, এ, ১২৭/৭৬ নং মোকদ্দমা অকার্য্যকর হইয়া পড়ে৷ বাদীপক্ষ নিরুপায় হইয়া মহামান্য হাইকের্ট ডিভিশনে উল্লেখিত অবস্থা বর্ননা করিয়া মামলাঢি পুনঃ দাখিলের শর্তে প্ৰত্যাহারের অনুমতি প্রার্থনা করিয়া ১১-৩-৮০ তারিখে আবেদন প্ত্রে জমা দেন এবং এ খুলনার ফিরিয়া আসেন৷শুনানী অন্তে মহামান্য হাইকোর্ট ডিভশন ৭-৪-৮০ তারিখের আদেশে আবেদনপত্রটি মনজুর করেন ৷”

<u>17. On the question of limitation some decision may be referred to. The case of Yalpi Virupakshappa vs Chowdireddi Veeravbhadra Gowd, AIR 1943 Madras 80, the case of Mohanlal Baherti vs Moulvi Tabizuddin Ahmed, AIR 1939 Calcutta 625, the case of Achut Dadaji Joshi vs Parashram Vasudev Mogre AIR 1938 281 and in the case of Sadayatan Pande vs (Firm) Ram Chandra Gopal, AIR 1934 688 wherein it is held that section 14 of the Limitation Act cannot be invoked to save limitation for subsequent suit.'</u>

18. In this suit we have seen that cause of action of the suit arose in 1962 and this suit having been filed in 1980 is barred by limitation. We find merit in the rule.

19. In the result, the rule is made absolute without any order as to costs.

20. Judgment and decree passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 1st Court, Khulna decreeing Title Suit No. 200 of 1980 is set aside and those passed by the learned Sub-ordinate Judge, 1st Court, Khulna in title Suit No. 200 of 1980 is restored.

Send down the lower court records. Communicate this judgment at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Gour Gopal Saha, J: This rule is directed against the order dated 18.6.1987 passed by the Assistant Judge, Lohagarah in Misc. Case No. 51 of 1987 by which the ex-parte decree dated 11.4.1979 passed by the Subordinate Judge, Jessore in Title Suit No. 91 of 1970 subsequently re-numbered as Title Suit No. 159 of 1987 was set aside.

2. Relevant facts, in short, for the purpose of the case are that the petitioners as plaintiffs filed a suit in the Court of the Subordinate Judge, Jessore, being Title Suit No. 91 of 1970 which was subsequently re-numbered as Title Suit No. 159 of 1987 on transfer for a declaration that the compromise decree passed in Title Suit No. 152 of 1969 is fraudulent collusive illegal, void and not binding upon the plaintiffs. Eventually the said suit was decreed ex-parte on 11.4.79. Thereafter defendant opposite party No. 1 Shaikh Bazlur Rahman filed on 11.5.1979 an application under Order 9 Rule 13 read with section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure for setting aside the aforesaid ex-parte decree on the ground that he was prevented by sufficient cause from appearing before the Court when the suit was taken up for ex-parte disposal whereupon Misc. Case No. 69 of 1979 was started. Unfortunately, the said case was dismissed for default on 23.11.82. Thereafter defendant opposite party No. 1 filed an application for review under Order 47 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure whereupon Misc. Case No. 153 of 1983 was started. The aforesaid review application was filed for setting aside the order dated 23.11.82 by which Misc. Case No. 69 of 1979 under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was dismissed for default. In the meantime, because of the creation of the Court of Assistant Judge at Lohagarah as a result of reorganisation of the Courts the case was transferred to the Court of the Assistant Judge. Lohagarah for disposal and the learned Assistant Judge, Lohagara by his order dated 16.6.1986 dismissed Misc. Case 'No. 153 of 1983 for default. Thereafter on 13.4.87 defendant opposite party No. 1 filed an application before the Assistant Judge, Lohagarah under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure on 16.6.86 for setting aside the dismissal of Misc. Case No. 156 of 1987 for default on the ground that he had no knowledge about the transfer of the case from Jessore to the Court of the Assistant Judge, Lohagara and no notice was given to him on the transfer of the aforesaid case from Jessore to Lohagarah.

3. The learned Assistant Judge by his order dated 3.5.87 allowed the aforesaid application of the defendant opposite party under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure setting aside the order of dismissal of Misc. Case No. 156 of 1985 for default and restored Misc. Case No. 156 of 1985 to its original file and number fixing 20.5.87 for steps. Thereafter by order dated 3.6.87 the learned Assistant Judge allowed Misc. Case No. 156 of 1985 under Order 47 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure and set aside the order dated 23.11.82 dismissing Misc. Case No. 69 of 1979 under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure, Subsequently, by the impugned order dated 18.6.1987 the learned Assistant Judge allowed the case under Order 9 rule 13 Of the Code of Civil Procedure and set aside the ex-parte decree dated 11.4.1979. Being aggrieved by, this order the petitioners moved this Court and obtained the present Rule.

4. Mr. Shumsul Huda the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioners submits that the learned Assistant Judge evidently erred in law in setting aside the order dated 16.6.86 and restoring Misc. Case No. 156 of 1985 to its original file and number acting under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure behind the back and beyond the knowledge of the petitioners and the same has resulted in error in the impugned decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submits that the learned Assistant Judge also erred in law in allowing Misc. Case No. 156 of 1985 by order dated 3.6.87 whereby the dismissal of the case under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure for default on 23.11.82 was set aside without hearing the petitioners and the same has occasioned failure of justice. The learned Advocate also submits that in view of the fact the impugned order dated 18.6.87 setting aside the ex-parte decree dated 11.4.79 in Title Suit No. 91 of 1970 subsequently renumbered as Title Suit No. 159 of 1987 was made beyond the knowledge of the petitioners without al fording them any opportunity of being, the same is liable to be set aside in the interest of justice.

5. Mr. Abdur Razzaque the learned Advocate appearing for opposite party No. 1 on the other hand submits that the learned Assistant Judge was perfectly justified in passing the impugned order and it does not suffer from any legal infirmity to justify interference by this Court exercising revisional power under section 115(5) of the Code of Civil Procedure.

6. The learned Advocate for the petitioners has placed before me the impugned Order as well as the application under Order 9 Rule 13 read with section 115 of the Code of Civil Procedure whereupon Misc. Case No. 69 of 1979 was started. This application has been marked as Annexure 'B' to the petition the order dated 23.11.82 dismissing Misc. Case No. 69 of 1979 for default, the application of defendant opposite party No. 1 under Order 47 Rule 1 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for review of the order dated 23.11.82 whereupon Misc. Case No. 156 of 1985 was started the order dated 16.6.86 by which Misc. Case No. 56 of 1985 for review was dismissed for default. the order dated 23.5.87 by which the learned Assistant Judge, Lohagarah allowed the case of the defendant opposite party No. 1 under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure after setting aside the order of dismissal dated 16.6.86 and restoring Misc. Case No. 156 of 1985 to its original file and number fixing 20.5.87 for steps, the order dated 3.6.87 by which the order dated. 23.11.87 dismissing the defendants case under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure in Misc. Case No. 69 of 1979 was set aside and the original Misc. Case was revived. From these it is clearly found that the learned Assistant Judge, Lohagarah by his order dated 16.6.86 dismissed Misc. Case No. (Review Case) 156 of 1985 for default for failing to take necessary steps. There is nothing on record to indicate that after Misc. Case No. 56 of 1985 was transferred from Jessore to the Court of the Assistant Judge, Lohagara, the parties were informed of the transfer of the said case from Jessore to Lohagara. In the facts and circumstances of the case it cannot be said with any amount of certainty that the petitioners of Misc. Case No.156 of 1985 had any knowledge about the transfer of his case from Jessore to Lohagara requiring him to take necessary steps for want of which Misc. Case No. 156 of 1985 was dismissed for default. It also appears that the learned Assistant Judge on the application of the defendant opposite party No. 1 under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure praying for setting aside the dismissal of the case for default ex-parte set aside the dismissal order dated 16.6.86 without serving any notice upon the petitioners and re-stored Misc. Case No.56 of 1985 to its original file and number behend their back and beyond their knowledge. It is also evident that by the subsequent order dated 3.6.87 the learned Assistant Judge, Lohagara set aside the order dated 3.6.87 setting aside the order dated 23.11.82 by which Misc. Case No. 69 of 1979 under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure was set aside and the case was re-stored to its original file and number. This order was also passed in the absence of the plaintiff-petitioners. There is nothing on record to show that they had any opportunity to have their say in the matter. Similarly the impugned order dated 18.6.87 allowing Misc. Case under Order 9 Rule 13 of the Code of Civil Procedure after setting aside the ex-parte decree dated 11.4.79 was passed ex-parte without affording any opportunity to the plaintiff-petitioners of being heard.

7. From the reading of aforesaid orders and in consideration of the facts and circumstances of the case. I am constrained to hold that the learned Assistant Judge, Lohagara committed a chain of illegalities beginning from dismissing Misc. Case No. 156 of 1985 by order dated 16.6.86 for allegedly not taking steps till the passing of the impugned order dated 18.6.87 without affording the petitioners any opportunity of being heard. This clearly indicates a complete lack of application of the judicial mind on the part of the learned Assistant Judge in the facts and circumstances of the case and the law bearing on the subject and the same has occasioned failure of justice.

<u>8. It is well-settled that when an order either contested or ex-parte is passed by any Court determining a matter before him a valuable tight accrues to the opposite party and that legal right cannot be taken away without affording such party an opportunity of being heard. In our case under review, the learned Assistant Judge merrily went on passing one order after another in the absence of the opposite parties taking away their valuable legal right without ensuring that necessary opportunities were given to them to have their say in the relevant matters. Such a course is never contemplated in law as it clearly militates against the principle of natural justice. The unfortunate procedure adopted by the learned Assistant Judge is not only arbitrary and illegal but also patently injudicious. It is thus found that the learned Assistant Judge erred in law in passing the impugned order dated 16.6.86 in dismissing Misc. Case No. 156 of 1985 for default in a most, casual manner. The order dated 3.5.87 allowing the application of the defendant-opposite party No. 1 under section 151 of the Code of Civil Procedure is equally arbitrary and illegal. Similarly the order dated 3.6.87 by which the learned Assistant Judge set aside the order dated 23.11.82 passed in Misc. Case No. 69 of 1979 under Order 9 Rule 13 of the plaintiffs-petitioners is also illegal and arbitrary and the same is the fate of the impugned order dated 18.6.87 by which the ex-parte decree dated 11.4.1979 was set aside, without affording the plaintiff-petitioners any opportunity of being heard.</u>

9. All these ultimately led to the passing of the impugned order dated 18.6.87 clearly indicating securing the non-application of a judicial mind by the learned Assistant Judge into the facts and circumstances and the law bearing on the subject and the same has occasioned failure of justice. In the facts and circumstances of the case, I am constrained to hold that orders dated 16.6.86. 3.5.87 and 3.6.87 passed in Misc. Case No. 165 of 1985 are illegal and arbitrary and the same cannot the allowed to stand in the interest of justice. I am also constrained to hold that the learned Assistant Judge. Lohagara clearly erred in law in passing the impugned order dated 18.6.87 in Misc. Case No. 51 of 1987 in setting aside the ex-parte decree dated 11.4.79 behind the back and beyond the knowledge of the petitioners and accordingly the said order is liable to be set aside. The submissions made by the learned Advocate for the petitioners merit consideration and the same are accordingly sustained.

10. In the result, the rule is made absolute without any order as to costs and the impugned order dated 18.6.87 passed in Misc. Case No. 51 of 1987 is set aside. Similarly, the orders dated 16.6.86. 3.5.67 and 3.6.87 passed in Misc. Case No. 156 of 1985 are also set aside in the interest of justice. The learned Assistant, Judge, Lohagara is directed to re-hear Misc. Case No. 156 of 1985 (Review case) on its merit after affording proper opportunities to the parties to represent their respective cases.

11. Since this is a very old case, the learned Assistant Judge, Lohagara is hereby directed to dispose of Misc. Case No. 156 of 1985 with utmost expediency preferably within 2 months from the date of the receipt of this order.

12. The order of stay granted earlier by this Court stands vacated. Send down the lower Court records at once. Communicate this order to the learned Assistant Judge, Lohagara at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Sikder Maqbul Huq, J: This Rule was issued calling upon opposite party No. 1 Mrs. Arzuda Khatun to show cause as to why the order dated 12.11.1998 passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, Commercial Court No. 2, Dhaka in Title Suit No. 16 of 1992 should not be set aside.

2. Opposite party No. 1 instituted Title Suit No. 16 of 1992 against the petitioner namely Mrs. Nazma Begum and others for a declaration of her title to and recovery of khas possession in the suit property.

3. Her case, in short, is that she took lease of the suit property from the erstwhile Government of East Pakistan vide lease deed No. 6327 dated 5.10.1968 and since then she was possessing the same. During the war of liberation, she had to leave her house on the suit land leaving her deeds etc. there in order to save her life and on return after liberation found that the petitioner had illegally entered into the possession of the same. She failed in her attempts to recover possession of the property and thus she was constrained to bring the suit for declaration of her title to and recovery of possession of the suit property.

4. The present petitioner namely Mrs. Nazma Begum also instituted Title Suit No. 17 of 1992 for specific performance of a contract against opposite party No. 1 and others. Her contention is that opposite party No. 2, who was in possession of the suit property, abandoned the same during the liberation movement of Bangladesh whereupon she (the present petitioner) entered into the property and continued to occupy and enjoy the same openly in her own right and in 1979 AD opposite party No. 2, a legally constituted attorney of opposite party No. 1, came back and demanded possession of the suit property from the petitioner and ultimately entered into a contract to sell the same to her for a consideration of Tk. 25,000.00 and executed a deed of agreement on receipt of Tk. 24,000.00 as earnest money on behalf of opposite party No. 1 and thereafter refused to execute and register the promised sale deed in respect of the property. Both the suits were in respect of the self-same property.

5. The learned Subordinate Judge tried both the suits analogously on framing the following issues:-

“ ১। দেঃ ১৬/৯২ নং মোকদ্দমা এবং ১৭/৯২ নং মোকদ্দমাটি ২টি অত্রকারে ও প্রকারে চলিতে পারে কিনা?

২। অত্র মোকদ্দমা ২টি তামাদি দোষে বারিত কিনা?

৩। বিরেধিীর সম্পত্তি দেঃ ১৬/৯২ নং মোকদ্দমার বাদিনীর মূলে প্রাপ্ত হইয়াছিলেন কিনা এবং বিরোধীয় ভূমিতে ১৬/৯২ নং মোকদ্দ্মার বাদীনী স্বত্ব দখল আছে কিনা?

৪। বিরোধী সম্পর্কে দেঃ ১৬/৯২ নং মোকদ্দমার বাদীনী এবং ১৭/৯২ নং মোকদ্দমার ১নং বিবাদিনী আরজুদা থাতুন আশেক হোসেনের বরাবরে কোন আমমোক্ত নামা সম্পাদন করিয়া দিয়াছেন কিন?

৫। দেঃ ১৭/৯২ নং মোকদ্দমার বাদিনী নাজমা বেগমের বরাবরে আমমোক্ত নামা মুলে আশেক হোসেন ৩০/৫/৭৯ তারিখে কোন চুক্তি সম্পাদন করিয়াছেন কিনা?

৬। উভয় মোকদ্দমা বাদী পক্ষ তাদের প্রার্থীত মতে প্রতিকার পাইতে পারে কিনা?

6. Both the parties adduced oral and documentary evidence in support of their respective contentions and the learned Subordinate Judge after discussing the evidence adduced by the parties and the attending facts and circumstances of the case came to the conclusion that the alleged Amoktanama and the deed of the agreement in favour of the present petitioner is forged and fabricated and that no agreement as alleged was ever entered upon and thus the learned Subordinate Judge dismissed the suit for specific performance of the contract. On the other hand, the learned Subordinate Judge. after discussing the material evidence on record and considering the facts and circumstances of the case, came to the conclusion that the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 16 of 1992 has succeeded in proving her case and decided to decree the suit. It may here be mentioned that the learned Subordinate Judge observed in the body of the judgment"

“এমতাবস্থায় ৩-৬ নং বির্চায বিষয়গুলি দেঃ ১৬/৯২ নং মামলার বাদিনী আরজুদা খাতুনের পক্ষে গুহিত হইল এবং দেঃ ১৭/৯২ নং মামলার বাদিনী নাজমা বেগমের বিরুদ্ধে গৃহিত হইল।

7. Thus it is apparent on the face of the record that the learned Subordinate Judge intended to decree in full Title Suit No. 16 of 1992 and also to dismiss in full Title Suit 17 of 1992 but the learned Subordinate Judge passed the order portion of the judgment in the following terms.

“অত্র দেঃ ১৬/৯২ নং মোকদ্দমাটি দোতরফা সূত্রে ১নং বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে এবং অন্যান্য বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে একতরফা সূত্রে বিনা খরচায় ডিক্রি প্রদান করা হইল এবং নাঃ জমিতে বাদিনীর স্বাত্ব ঘোষিত হইল। পক্ষান্তরে দেঃ ১৭/৯২ নং মোকদ্দমাটি দোতরফা সূত্রে ১নং বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে এবং অন্যান্য বিবাদীর বিরুদ্ধে একতরফা সূত্রে বিনা খরচায় ডিসমিশ করা হইল।”

8. It is thus also apparent on the face of the record that the order portion of the judgment does not represent the intention of the learned Subordinate Judge as well as the decision he took in the body of the judgment. It may further be mentioned that the plaintiff of Title Suit No. 16 of 1992 was admittedly out of possession from long before the institution of the suit and as such there could be no question of passing the decree of declaration of title without any consequential relief in her favour.

9. The learned Subordinate Judge passed the judgment on 27.9.98 where after the decree was prepared and signed on 6.10.98. The decree was drawn in accordance with the order portion of the judgment i.e. in the decree plaintiffs title was declared and nothing was said about the prayer for recovery of khas possession. Opposite party No.1 Arzuda Khatun on 8.11.98 filed an application before the learned Subordinate Judge praying for amendment of the judgment and the decree incorporating the relief of khas possession in her favour and the learned Subordinate Judge by his order dated 12.11.98 allowed the prayer for amendment of the judgment and decree accordingly and it appears from the record that the judgment and the decree were amended.

10. Mr. Faruque Ahmed, the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner, submitted that there is a distinction between the clerical or arithmetical mistake in the judgment and decree or order and judicial mistakes crept therein. The learned Advocate further submitted that the mistake corrected by the learned Subordinate Judge does not fall within the ambit of clerical or arithmetical mistake or accidental slip or omission. In other words, it has been submitted that the mistakes corrected by the learned Subordinate Judge is not at all covered by section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure and as such the learned Subordinate Judge committed an error of law in correcting the concerned judgment and the decree resulting in error in the decision occasioning failure of justice. The learned Advocate further submitted that the learned Subordinate Judge also committed an illegality in passing the impugned order without serving any notice upon the petitioner.

11. The learned Advocate appearing for the opposite party, however, submitted that the Court can correct any error or omission covered by section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure even suo motu and as such it is not obligatory upon the Court to give notice upon the defendants before amendment of an accidental mistake or omission. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties in support of his contention has referred to the decision reported in DLR 22 130.

12. The learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner in support of his contention firstly referred to the definition of clerical error as given in Mitra's Legal and Commercial Dictionary, third edition page 158. The definition of clerical error as given in the said dictionary is as follows "A clerical error is one made in transcribing or other wise and it must be apparent on the face of the record and therefore capable of being corrected. It is in the nature of an inadvertent omission or mistake. The term 'clerical error' is distinguishable from a judicial error which can be corrected only on review or an appeal (Mansha Ram Vs. Taj Bhan, ILR(1961) 1 Punjab 728: AIR 1962 Punjab 110). Supply of omissions may be permissible if they are in the nature of clerical omission but certainly such omissions as would demand judicial consideration or determination are beyond the scope of the expressions. Bangaru Reddy Vs. State, AIR 1959 AP95.

13. "Clerical or arithmetical mistakes in judgments, decrees or orders may be corrested by the Court under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure."

The above definition also has made a distinction between clerical and judicial error about which further discussion will be made in a subsequent paragraph.

14. The learned advocate for the petitioner referring to AIR 1935 (Calcutta) 619 has candidly submitted that clerical or arithmetical mistake or an error arising from an accidental slip or omission creeping in the judgment; decree and order can be corrected provided in doing so no injustice is done to the other side. It has further been held in the said reported case that though no notice is necessary for amendment of decree by the Court it would be unfair to allow a decree to be amended without an opportunity being given to the party which will be affected by the amendment. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has further referred to AIR 1962 (Punjab) 110 wherein it has been held that a 'clerical error' is one made in transcribing or otherwise, and it must be apparent on the face of the record; and, therefore, capable of being corrected. It is in the nature of an inadvertent omission or mistake. The term `clerical error' is distinguishable from "Judicial error' which can be corrected only on review or an appeal. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has also referred, to a decision reported in 39 CWN page 1295 wherein it has been held that it is unfair to allow a decree to be amended without any opportunity being given to the party which will be affected by the amendment although under the present Civil Procedure Code, no notice is necessary for the purpose of the amendment of a decree. It has further been held that "The Court which passed a decree can amend it in two cases only, (1) when there is a clerical or arithmetical mistake or slip and (ii) where the Court itself finds that the decree does not correctly represent what was decided or intended to he decided, provided the amendment can be made without injustice."

15. The learned Advocate for the petitioner has yet referred to another decision reported in 1968 A.I.R. page 66, wherein it has been held that omission to decide if mesne profits to be granted or not, while passing decree mistake not of accidental or clerical nature and as such cannot be corrected under sections 151 and 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure and relief of the aggrieved party lies by way of revision and appeal. Facts of the said case are not applicable to the facts and circumstances of the case before the. Besides it has subsequently been held in some cases that the Court can amend the decree allowing mesne profit if not allowed earlier due to accidental omission. Therefore the above cited decision does not in any way help the petitioner.

16. The learned Advocate for the opposite parties has referred to the decision reported in 22 DLR page 130 wherein it has been held that the language of section 152 is wide enough to include any accidental slip or omission of which the source may be somewhere other than the judgment and the decree. This decision is also not directly on the point before me and as such I refrain from discussing the same or making any comment on it.

17. It has been held in the case reported in 29 DLR page 81, "Mistake due to accidental slip or omission or inadvertence can he set right by the Court." In the said reported case it has been held where a mistake crept into the description of an item of property in the plaint-schedule and the mistake has been carried over in the decree, the Court certainly has powers to correct the error in the decree if the Court is satisfied that the mistake made by the parties in the pleadings is an accidental slip or omission or is due to inadvertence and it is palpable that nobody can possibly have any doubt as to what the parties meant." Thus it is apparent from this decision that the scope qt. section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure is wide enough to include any mistake or omission due to accidental slip or inadvertence and the Court can even take into consideration any mistake by the party committed in the pleadings.

18. It has been held in the case reported in 28 DLR, 392 that the test to determine whether the slip or omission is accidental or not is to see whether the judgment, decree or order, as it stands, represents the intention of the judge at the time he made it and if it does, then a mistake in it cannot be treated as an accidental slip or omission. But in the facts and circumstances of the instant case, I have earlier mentioned that the judgment or decree does not represent the intention of the judge at the time of making it. I have stated the facts and circumstances of the case in view of which there is no scope to say that the judgment and decree amended in way represented the intention of the judge when he made them.

19. It has further been held that the decree should be consistent with the plaint in the absence of an indication that a particular relief has been refused. The plaint contained prayers (1) for cancellation of kabala alleged to have been executed fraudulently and (2) for relief of recovery of possession of property, subject matter of the Kabala. The suit was decreed by the Court. The Kabala was cancelled but that relief of recovery of possession was not mentioned in the decree. Omission, in the circumstances, held, was inadvertent, which could be supplied under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure (PLD 1970 Dhaka 475). Thus where the directions as to costs were inadvertently omitted or when the directions as to mesne profit were accidentally omitted the decree was set right by adding such directions.

<u>20. If a matter decided by the Court is not included in the decree, the omission may be corrected on application for amendment of the decree (PLD 1963 SC 265). Every Court has an inherent power to vary or amend its own decree or to order so as to carry out its own meaning. It would be perfectly shocking if the Court could not rectify its own error.</u>

21. Where the plaintiff brought a suit for partition and sought relief for the same, the trial Court decreed the suit partly but the High Court on appeal being misled inadvertently omitted to pass a decree for partition and instead granted decree for joint possession of property (for which there was no prayer). Decree of the Court was liable to be amended in the circumstances of the case.

22. Court can even suo motu correct its own mistake under section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure. The concerned mistake can not be termed as judicial mistake as there was nothing to be determined by the learned Subordinate Judge before passing the impugned order as he decided all the issues in favour of the plaintiff. It may be mentioned that one of the issues framed by him was to the effect that whether the plaintiff is entitled to the decree as prayed for and it has been decided in the affirmative. Thus the mistake sought to be corrected, in view of the forgoing discussion, cannot termed to be a judicial mistake and the same is an accidental slip or omission due to inadvertence of the Judge, which is covered by section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

23. In view of the above discussion, I find that the mistakes in the judgment and decree were due to inadvertence amounting to accidental slip and omission and this clearly comes under the purview of section 152 of the Code of Civil Procedure.

24. I have been informed at the time of hearing this revisional application by the learned Advocate appearing for the petitioner that the petitioner has also preferred an appeal against the connected judgment and decree. It is apparent from the earlier discussion that the petitioner would not be prejudiced by the impugned order amending the judgment and decree. On the other hand, the decree originally passed in favour of opposite party No. 1 declaring her title without recovery of khas possession will be of no use to her. The learned Subordinate Judge, as a matter of prudence, ought to have served a copy of the petition for amendment upon the petitioner or upon her advocate but his failure to do so cannot be said to have rendered the impugned order illegal and void.

25. A mistake apparent on the face of the record has been corrected and the petitioner does not appear to have been prejudiced by it. Apparently no injustice has been done to the petitioner by the impugned order and the same does not call for any interference.

26. The learned Subordinate Judge, in view of the facts and circumstances of the case, has committed no illegally in passing the impugned order resulting in an error in the decision occasioning failure of justice.

27. In the result, the rule is discharged without any order as to costs. The order of stay granted earlier by this court stands vacated.

Communicate the order at once.

End.

full_judgment:
Mohammad Gholam Rabbani, J: This appeal has arisen out of the following circumstances:-

Appellant Shamsun Nahar alias Falani was the principal defendant in Title Suit No.325 of 1987 instituted by the respondent no. 1 to 8 Ahmed Peari and others in the 3rd Court of Subordinate Judge, Dhaka. The suit was for declaration of title to and recovery of khas possession of a four-storied building at 93/ka, Arambagh within the city of Dhaka.

2. Ultimately the suit was taken up for peremptory hearing on 26.2.92 when P.W.1 Ahmed Sharif was examined in part and certain documents of the plaintiffs were marked as exhibits. Then the peremptory hearing was adjourned to 28.3.92. But on that date the principal defendant and thereafter on two adjourned dates the plaintiff took adjournments. However on 15.6.92 examination-in-chief of the P.W.1 was completed and P.W.1 was cross-examined partly by the principal defendant.

3. Subsequently on 14.9.92 principal defendant filed an application for expunging the deposition of the, P.W.1 on the ground that he had died. Learned Subordinate-Judge rejected the application by the order dated 4.2.93 and against thereof principal defendant obtained rule from the High Court Division in Civil Revision No. 2113 of 1993 and got the further proceedings of the suit stayed till the disposal of the rule. High Court Division discharged the rule by the judgment and order dated 5.7.94.

4. Copy of the judgment passed by the High Court Division was received by the trial Court on 5.9.94 and on that date learned Subordinate Judge passed the following order:-

“মহামান্য সুপ্রীমকোর্ট বাংলাদেশ হাইকোর্ট বিভাগ, ঢাকা হইতে ৫-৩-৯৭ইং তারিখের ১০৯৯-ভি নং স্মারকের মাধ্যমে সিভিল রিভিশন নং ২১১৩/৯৩ এর আদেশের কপি পাওয়া গেল দেখিলাম। ৪-২-৯৪ তারিখের আদেশ বহাল রাখা হইয়াছে। আগামী ইং ২৮/৯/৯৪ বক্রী সাক্ষী গ্রহনের জন্য রহিল।”

5. It is to be noticed that except the first sentence other sentences were written by the learned Subordinate Judge himself. On 28.9.94 and thereafter on several adjourned dates principal defendant did neither file hajira nor appear. Ultimately learned Subordinate Judge decreed the suit by the judgment and decree dated 7.5.95.

6. On 30.11.95 principal defendant filed Miscellaneous Case No.48 of 1995 under Or. 9, r. 13, C.P.C. for setting aside the decree alleging it as an ex-parte decree. In paragraph 5 of her application in the case principal defendant alleged as hereunder:

“বিবাদী পক্ষ উক্ত দেওয়ানী মোকদ্দমার শুনানীর তারিখ সম্পর্কে ওয়াকেবহাল না থাকার কারনে মোকদ্দমাটি এক তরফা ভাবে ডিক্রী হওয়ায় বিবাদীনি মজহর পক্ষের অপূরনীয় ক্ষতির কারন হইয়াছে।

7. Learned Subordinate Judge, summarily dismissed the case holding it as not maintainable under Order 9, rule 13 C.P.C. by the order dated 10.8.96 on the ground that the suit was decreed on contest obviously under Order 17 rule 3. C.P.C. Hence this appeal by the principal defendant.

Heard the learned advocates and perused the records. Rule 2 and 3 of Order 17 C.P.C. run as follows:-

"2. Where on any day to which the hearing of the suit is adjourned, the parties or any or them fail to appear the court may proceed to dispose of the suit in one of the modes directed in that behalf by Order IX or make such other order as it thinks fit."

"3. Where, any party to a suit to whom time has been granted fails to produce his evidence, or to cause the attendance of his witnesses, or to perform any other act necessary to the further progress of the suit, for which time has been allowed, the Court may, notwithstanding such default, proceed to decide the suit forthwith."

8. Difference between r. 2 and r. 3 is by now well-settled. Rule 2 contemplates absence of both the parties or one of the parties at an adjourned hearing no matter for what purpose the adjournment was made and the court may proceed under rule 3 or rule 6 or rule 8 of Order 9 as the case may be Rule 3 applies only if the previous adjudgment was granted for any of the purposes mentioned in this rule and not to a general adjournment. Therefore elements required to proceed under rule 3 are: (I) the adjournment was at the instance of a party and (ii) there are materials on the record to decide the suit.

<u>9. In the instant suit, we find, the learned Subordinate Judge committed two errors of law in applying rule 3. None of the parties took adjournment on his own application for taking certain steps as mentioned in rule 3 e.g. to produce witnesses or to do any specified act. When the court itself adjourns the suit for production of evidence the adjournment does not bring into operation rule 3. In this case before us neither rule 2 nor rule 3 was applicable. Learned Subordinate Judge did not adjourn the hearing of the suit, he only fixed a date for production of evidence consequent to the High Court Division's vacating its order of staying the further proceedings of the suit.</u>

<u>10. Secondly learned Subordinate Judge ought to have informed the learned Advocates of the parties about his order dated 5.9.94. From the order quoted above we do not find the necessary sentence "Inform the parties through their learned advocates". Although the order was written by the learned Subordinate Judge him. We accept the ground quoted above of the principal defendant for restoring the suit.</u>

11. A full bench of the Allahabad High Court in a case (Munnalal V. Jaiprakash) reported in AIR 1970 All 257 held that whenever it is possible to construe the order within the provisions of rule 2, it should be done so and even when the court purports to act under rule 3 if the circumstances are such that an order under Order 9 read with rule 2 of Order 17 would be legally Justified and the actual order passed could be legally passed under Order 9 read with Order 17, rule 2 it is permissible to entertain an application for restoration under Order 9. We concur with this decision.

12. Thus we find that not only the impugned order dismissing the miscellaneous case summarily should be set aside, but the miscellaneous case should also be allowed to shorten the sufferings of the principal defendant.

13. In the result this appeal is allowed without cost. Impugned order dated 10.8.96, passed by the learned Subordinate Judge, 3rd Court Dhaka, in Miscellaneous Case No. 48 of 1995 is set aside and the case is restored to its original file and number. The Miscellaneous case is allowed without cost. Judgment and decree dated 24.5.95 passed in Title Suit No. 325 of 1987 are set aside and the suit is restored to its original file and number to be disposed of in accordance with law as quickly as possible preferably within three months from date. Connected Civil Rule No. 269 (fm) of 1996 is disposed of accordingly without cost.

Send down the L.C. records at once.

End.
